card.name: Wanaragua
card.era: Emerged 18th c. during slavery; costume/disguise origins tied to St. Vincent resistance (pre-1797)
card.tagline: Garifuna masked warrior dance of resistance, where the dancer leads the drum.
card.profile: Wanaragua (Garifuna for 'mask'; also 'Jankunu' or 'John Canoe') is a masked dance performed by men during the Christmas-New Year season, traveling house to house. Dancers wear pink/white wire masks with European features (satirizing colonial slave masters), tall crepe-paper crowns, mirrors and feathers, ribboned women's-style costumes, and cowrie/shell knee rattles, dancing to the primero and segunda drums while women sing as 'gayusas' (chorus). It is one of the few dances where the drummers follow the dancer's movements rather than the reverse (MyBelize.Net; UNICEF Belize).
card.insight: Wanaragua is the most culturally significant of Garifuna masked performances - an embodied performance of resistance and resilience commemorating ancestors (Constellations, F. Arzu Carmichael; Oliver N. Greene Jr.). It falls under the UNESCO 2001/2008 Garifuna inscription.
